text: John Edward Broadbent (March 21, 1936 – January 11, 2024) was a Canadian social-democratic politician and political scientist. He served as leader of the New Democratic Party (NDP) from 1975 to 1989 and was a member of Parliament from 1968 to 1990 and from 2004 to 2006. He led the NDP through four federal elections, during which the party's parliamentary representation grew from 17 to 43 seats by the 1988 federal election. Broadbent was born in Oshawa, Ontario, the son of Percy, who worked at General Motors, and Mary (Welsh) Broadbent, a homemaker. In 1961, he married Yvonne Yamaoka, a Japanese Canadian town planner whose family had been interned during World War II; they divorced in 1967. He earned a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in political science from the University of Toronto in 1966 with a thesis titled "The Good Society of John Stuart Mill," under the supervision of C.B. Macpherson. He entered Parliament in 1968, winning the riding of Oshawa—Whitby by fifteen votes over Progressive Conservative MP Michael Starr in a close three-way race, beginning his service in the 28th Canadian Parliament. After Tommy Douglas retired, Broadbent was eliminated on the second ballot in the 1971 leadership convention, with David Lewis becoming leader; Lewis stepped down in 1974 due to poor electoral results and ill health. Broadbent won the 1975 leadership election and led the party through four federal elections. In the 1979 federal election, the NDP increased its seat count from 17 to 26; in 1980, it rose from 27 to 32 seats. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau offered Broadbent a coalition government after the 1980 election, which he declined. In 1984, the NDP secured 30 seats, ten behind the Liberals led by John Turner. Broadbent consistently ranked first in personal popularity among federal party leaders, and in 1987 became the first NDP leader to place the party first in public opinion polling since the party's founding. Some analysts predicted the NDP could become the primary opposition to the Brian Mulroney-led Progressive Conservatives, though Broadbent supported the Meech Lake Accord, which caused internal dissent. In the 1988 federal election, the NDP won 43 seats, a record not surpassed until 2011 when it reached 103 seats. Despite strong polling, the NDP remained third behind the Liberals and faced criticism for not making opposition to the Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement a central campaign issue. Broadbent served as vice-president of Socialist International from 1979 to 1989, during which Willy Brandt was president, and as director of the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development from 1990 to 1996. He stepped down as NDP leader at the 1989 Winnipeg Convention, succeeded by Audrey McLaughlin, and resigned his Oshawa seat that year; Michael Breaugh won the 1990 Oshawa by-election for the NDP. After his retirement, the federal NDP declined in popularity until Jack Layton took over in 2003. In 1993, he was named an Officer of the Order of Canada and promoted to Companion in 2001. He spent 1996–1997 as a Fellow at All Souls College, University of Oxford. At Layton's invitation, Broadbent returned to politics in 2004, winning the riding of Ottawa Centre by defeating Liberal candidate Richard J. Mahoney, a close ally of Prime Minister Paul Martin. In the NDP shadow cabinet, he served as Critic for Democracy: Parliamentary & Electoral Reform, Corporate Accountability, and Child Poverty. On May 4, 2005, he announced he would not seek re-election in the 39th federal election to spend time with his wife Lucille, who died of cancer on November 17, 2006. In November 2008, Broadbent and former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien retired to negotiate a coalition between the Liberals and NDP, supported by the Bloc Québécois, to replace Stephen Harper’s Conservative government—this would have been Canada’s first coalition since World War I—but the plan collapsed after Governor General Michaëlle Jean prorogued Parliament in December 2008 at Harper’s request. On June 17, 2011, Broadbent announced the creation of the Broadbent Institute, a policy think tank independent of the NDP, dedicated to exploring social-democratic policy, providing education, and training activists. Three months later, he endorsed Brian Topp in the 2012 leadership election. In 2017, he supported the campaign for a United Nations Parliamentary Assembly to promote democratic reform and accountability in the UN. In 2022, he published Seeking Social Democracy, a reflection on his life and career co-authored with Francis Abele, Jonathan Sas, and Luke Savage. Until his death, he was a fellow in the School of Policy Studies at Queen's University. In 1971, Broadbent married Franco-Ontarian widow Lucille Munroe, who died of cancer on November 17, 2006, at age 71. In 2014, he married Ellen Meiksins Wood, a Marxist historian and political theorist and professor at York University for three decades, who died of cancer at age 73 in January 2016. Broadbent died on January 11, 2024, at age 87. His state funeral on January 28 at Carleton Dominion-Chalmers Centre in Ottawa was the first Canadian state funeral for a party leader who had never been prime minister or leader of the official opposition. There is an Ed Broadbent fonds at Library and Archives Canada.
